name: All-over colour (single process)
how: Roots to ends in one shade; often refreshed at the roots only.
client: One even colour from roots to ends. Simple and polished, and the roots show as the hair grows.
stylist: Works for shades at or near the client's current visible level, or darker. Lifting more than a little needs a different technique. Best when the hair is evenly coloured and the target is at a similar or darker level. Predictable on healthy hair; the less the shade differs from the natural level, the softer the regrowth. Always check history and keep the skin test in the plan.

name: Gloss / glaze (tone refresh)
how: Applied over the whole head or to lengths and ends after lightening or between colour visits.
client: An easy, sheer colour or toner that adjusts tone and adds shine. It does not usually lift.
stylist: Can refresh ash, gold, copper or red tones between visits; cannot cover heavy grey or lighten. Suits any starting level. Good bridge between colour visits. Result depends heavily on porosity and the existing colour; sheer pigment shows most on lighter hair.

name: Foil highlights
how: Woven sections from near the root to the ends, usually with a defined root.
client: Sections of hair are lightened inside foils for a clear, bright, structured lift.
stylist: Pairs with beige, golden, honey, ash or platinum blondes on light to medium bases. Best when starting from level 3-7, healthy, little prior colour. Strong lift and control; the wider the contrast, the more visible the root line. Needs appointment and strand test.

name: Babylights
how: Micro-sections through the top and sides, close to the root.
client: Very fine, soft highlights like the natural lightness seen in children's hair.
stylist: Pairs with soft blondes (beige, sandy, honey, champagne) and with grey blending. Best when starting from level 4-7, healthy. Takes time because of the fine sectioning; a good fit for gentle brightness and for blurring early grey. Strand test first.

name: Lowlights
how: Through the mid-lengths to create dimension.
client: Strands deposited a few levels darker than the base to add depth or break up heavy highlights.
stylist: Pairs with honey, caramel, ash or copper to add dimension; helps grey blending. Suits most starting levels, but very dark hair has little room to go darker. Useful to re-balance over-lightened hair and to soften grey. Grey percentage and tone decide the shade.

name: Balayage
how: Painted on the surface, heavier toward the ends and around the face.
client: Colour painted by hand through the mid-lengths and ends, with a soft root, so it grows out gently.
stylist: Pairs with caramel, honey, beige, bronde and copper; suits nearly any base though very dark hair needs more stages. Best when starting from level 3-7, healthy. Amount of lift varies with base level. Lighter results on dark hair take longer and may need more than one visit; history and condition must be checked first.

name: Foilayage
how: Painted sections wrapped for greater lightening.
client: Painted like balayage, then wrapped in foil or film for a stronger, brighter lift.
stylist: Pairs with light blondes, honey, champagne, copper; useful when free-painted balayage would not lift enough. Best when starting from level 3-7, healthy. Wrapping gives stronger lift, so porous or fragile hair needs careful assessment. Same strand test and appointment requirement as other lightening.

name: Ombre
how: Distinct gradient from mid-lengths, with the natural root zone left.
client: A two-tone gradient: darker roots flowing to much lighter lengths and ends.
stylist: Pairs with caramel, honey, blonde, copper and vivid ends. Best when starting from level 2-6, healthy lengths. Strong contrast needs a lot of lifting at the lengths; ends can be dry or porous. Needs a healthy-hair assessment.

name: Sombre (soft ombre)
how: Subtle gradient; lengths and ends about two or three levels lighter than roots.
client: A softer ombre with a gentle fade between close tones.
stylist: Pairs with beige, caramel, honey, bronde and muted tones. Best when starting from level 3-6. Needs less lift than ombre; the shade is chosen to melt softly into the base.

name: Root shadow / root smudge
how: At the roots, softly blended into the lengths.
client: A slightly deeper colour at the roots that melts into the lengths, so regrowth shows less.
stylist: Pairs with blonde, silver and vivid lengths to cover regrowth and add depth. Best when starting from light lengths with natural roots. Good for extending visits; the shadow shade must match the client's natural level and tone.

name: Colour melt
how: Blending along each strand from root to ends.
client: Two or three shades blended smoothly so one flows into the next, without a visible line.
stylist: Pairs with multi-tone looks: brunette to caramel to blonde, or vivid blends. The right starting level depends on the target. Needs advanced blending skill. Final blend depends on base, porosity and chosen shades.

name: Money piece / face-framing
how: Front sections near the face, heavier at the front and thinner behind.
client: Brighter sections at the front that frame the face, while the rest of your colour stays as it is.
stylist: Pairs with any base; golden, honey, platinum or copper accent strands. Best when starting from level 3-7. The face frame draws attention, so the tone must suit the client's skin and preferences. Lighter pieces need regular toning.

name: Peekaboo / underlights
how: Underneath sections, often at the nape or behind the ears.
client: Hidden colour in the underlayer or nape that shows when hair moves or is styled up.
stylist: Pairs with vivid, copper or platinum accents under natural hair. Suits any starting level. Good where workplace rules limit visible colour; sectioning is the main time cost. Pre-lightening is needed for bright shades.

name: Grey blending
how: Fine lights and lowlights around the root zone or through the surface.
client: Lights and lowlights that blend with your natural grey instead of covering it, for a soft grow-out.
stylist: Pairs with the grey-blend shades, beige, sandy or soft brunette. Best when starting from about 20-60% grey. Often best at lower to middle grey percentages; tone, grey texture and desired visibility of grey decide the approach. A strand test is useful.

name: Grey coverage (root colour)
how: Roots only, with an occasional refresh of lengths.
client: Permanent colour applied to the regrowth to cover grey. Very resistant grey can need extra steps.
stylist: Pairs with level 3-7 natural-looking shades and a warm or neutral base. Best when starting from roots with grey. Percentage and texture of grey affect which formula is needed; very resistant grey may need extra steps. Skin test before every use.

client: A colourist's plan to put right colour that is patchy, banded, too dark, too brassy or damaged.
stylist: Depends on the case. Professional only: needs in-person assessment, strand test and realistic aims; outcomes are not promised and the sequence is decided case by case.

name: Vivid all-over colour
how: Roots to ends or lengths only, over a pre-lightened base.
client: A bright fashion colour all over, usually on hair that has been lightened first. It fades quickly.
stylist: Pastel shades need very pale bases; deeper vivids (cherry red, plum, midnight blue) can show on darker bases at lower brightness. Best when starting from level 8-10 or pre-lightened. Base level and previous colour decide the end result; bright colours on dark hair usually need lightening. Dyes may stain skin and fabrics.

name: Demi/semi-permanent refresh (tone-on-tone)
client: A gentle, tone-on-tone colour that revives depth and shine and fades without a hard line.
stylist: Pairs with any shade at or darker than the current level. Suits any starting level. A good test-drive for clients unsure about commitment; limited grey coverage (blends rather than covers).
